transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-21
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~68 minutes
Attendees: Eva (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Dina (Redwood Product), Sofia (EmberSea Head of ML), Derrick (Backend), Priya (Infra), Tom (CTO)

[00:00] Eva: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. This is Eva from Redwood, im gonna share the optimize console and then Marcus will go into batching and KV recs. uh if we could start with a quick intro from EmberSea?
[00:18] Sofia: Hi, I'm Sofia, head of ML. we've been prototyping a chat assistant and trying to get the inference costs under control. main asks: keep p95 latency under 400ms, and cut per-session token cost by ~30%.
[00:32] Tom: Tom here, CTO. we also need VPC/on-prem options or at least VPC peering for data residency.
[00:41] Eva: Great, that's helpful. quick agenda: cost-sim walkthrough, batching/kv tradeoffs, security Qs, next steps. Marcus?
[00:52] Marcus: thanks. i'll start with an overview of how batch sizing, concurrency, and prefix (KV) caching interact with token economics, then we'll demo the console's simulator.
[01:05] [01:05] Marcus: so, quick mental model: per-token cost has two pieces: compute/throughput amortized across batches, and per-request overhead for small requests. batching bigger sequences reduces compute per-token, but increases tail latency for single-shot low-latency calls. prefix/KV caching helps when you have repeated conversation history or system prompts — it saves compute by reusing past key/value states.
[01:35] Derrick: real question, how much hit-rate do we need to make KV prefetch worth it? our session churn is pretty high.
[01:44] Marcus: good Q. typical break-even depends on prompt size and average reuse. in the console sim i put a few scenarios: if average reuse is >30% for the first 256 tokens, you often see >20% cost savings after accounting for prefetch cost. but if churn is 80% and lookahead fetches are wasted, you'll see negative returns.
[02:06] [02:06] Eva: and the console gives a heatmap — you can sweep batch size, concurrency, and prefetch window to see unit economics. i'll pull that up now.
[02:18] [02:18] Eva: (screen) okay here's the savings matrix: x-axis is batch size, y-axis is prefix window length, color = delta in $/1k requests. note the darker blue in the mid-range — that's the sweet spot for your prompt mix.
[02:35] Priya: quick sec — firewall/VPC question: if we run a sandbox, what do you need from our network team?
[02:42] Marcus: mostly peering or a single egress whitelist. we'll provide IP ranges, and we support customer-managed peering for private deployments. for hosted even with VPC peering you can keep audit logs separate.
[02:56] Sofia: can you clarify the prefetch mechanism? is it synchronous or async? i.e., does it block user latency?
[03:02] Marcus: prefetch is an async background step triggered when session activity looks likely to continue; but we support both sync prefetch and opportunistic prefetch. sync will add a small latency but gives best hit-rate, opportunistic is low-impact but sometimes misses windows.
[03:18] [03:18] Derrick: and how do you price the prefetch tokens? like are they billed the same as consumed tokens?
[03:23] Eva: prefetch tokens are accounted for in the cost model — in the sim we subtract wasted prefetch tokens from savings. on the bill, it's token usage but we break out lookahead/kv prefetch usage in the console for transparency.
[03:40] Marcus: also important: our runtime can downgrade to a cheaper quantized model on fallback to keep tail-latency and availability. that affects the cost columns in the spreadsheet; we have a model-variant routing policy you can tune.
[03:55] [03:55] Tom: security checklist: SOC2, KMS, RBAC, audit logs — do you have docs?
[04:01] Eva: yes — we'll drop SOC2 evidence and our private deployment checklist. support for KMS/HSM for private is available.
[04:09] Marcus: i'll attach the architecture sketch for VPC peering as well.
[04:14] [04:14] Marcus: now demoing the cost-sim. so you can import a sample prompt mix or upload a CSV of session lengths and token counts. i'm loading the EmberSea sample you shared earlier — thanks.
[04:29] Sofia: yep that was the file. curious to see assumptions on p95 latency and concurrency.
[04:35] Marcus: here we set latency target 400ms p95, concurrency target of 120 users. the sim computes expected throughput and picks an autoscaling curve — the output shows monthly cost and per-request median.
[04:48] [04:48] Marcus: you can toggle KV prefetch: watch the right panel — with a 128-token prefetch window we see 18% saving in this workload; increase to 256 tokens and saving hits 24% but CPU utilization goes up by 12%.
[05:05] Derrick: is that utilization on GPUs? like does it assume a specific instance type?
[05:09] Marcus: yes we parameterize by instance SKU; the sim current run uses an A100-80GB equivalent config. you can change to cheaper 80GB-quantized variants and it re-simulates.
[05:20] [05:20] Sofia: curious about cold-starts and KV bootstrapping for new sessions — how long before you get meaningful hit-rates?
[05:28] Marcus: usually need a few repeated interactions; with system prompts or templated prefixes you can see hits immediately for the prefix tokens. session-level caches take longer. console provides a session heatmap of expected warmup.
[05:42] [05:42] Eva: anecdote: one customer cut token spend by ~31% by combining 192-batch steady-state with 200-token prefix prefetch and a 2-tier model fallback.
[05:50] Tom: interesting. about concurrency — our product has spikes at 11am and 8pm. how does autoscaling and burst capacity handle that?
[05:59] Marcus: we have burst pools and can route to a lower-cost model variant under heavy load. autoscaler has cooldowns you can tune; the sim includes a spike simulation.
[06:12] [06:12] Priya: any experimental features to increase hit-rates? e.g., compacting history, canonicalization?
[06:18] Marcus: yes — prefix canonicalization and deterministic template normalization help. we also recommend grouping similar sessions to a shard to increase reuse. some of that is manual; we're adding console helpers for clustering common prefixes.
[06:31] [06:31] Derrick: question on accuracy regressions when using quantized models — how do we monitor quality?
[06:37] Dina: we have eval hooks in the console. you can bind prompt sets and run regression alerts when quality drops beyond a threshold. we show delta metrics and examples.
[06:48] [06:48] Marcus: also we can A/B route a fraction of traffic to the quantized model to measure impact before rolling out.
[06:55] Sofia: nice. if we run the sandbox, can we get the console metrics mapped to our Grafana?
[07:01] Eva: yes, we have export hooks and can push traces to your ingestion endpoint; we also support OTLP and prometheus exporters.
[07:10] [07:10] (screen) Marcus: now switching to the heatmap builder — you can drag to choose a target latency and the optimizer suggests a pair (batch size, prefetch window) that hits your target while minimizing cost.
[07:25] Tom: the recommendation engine — is that rules-based or learned from live telemetry?
[07:30] Marcus: hybrid — rule heuristics are seeded from benchmarks, and we refine recommendations using live telemetry if you enable anonymized usage insights.
[07:40] [07:40] Derrick: any gotchas for conversational systems that do function calling / tool access?
[07:45] Marcus: function calling changes token shape — you sometimes get very bursty token emission when tools return big blobs. for that we recommend conservative prefetch and smaller batch sizes to keep latency acceptable; the sim has an option to model tool-return variance.
[07:59] [07:59] Eva: small demo of CLI export — this csv shows cost columns split by compute, prefetch, and fallback. i'll attach it after the call.
[08:08] Sofia: thanks. do you have guidance on measuring real hit-rates in production?
[08:13] Marcus: instrument the logs with KV hit/miss counters per session and sample the top sessions. console can ingest those logs and re-run the sim with observed hit-rates for more accurate projections.
[08:27] [08:27] Priya: about encryption — if we use KMS can Redwood see plaintext?
[08:32] Eva: for hosted the control plane handles keys but you can opt for customer-managed keys; for private on-prem deployments you keep keys and we never see plaintext. we'll include the KMS section in the security pack.
[08:45] [08:45] Marcus: a deeper technical note: KV cache is stored in RAM with an eviction TTL; in private deployments you can persist checkpoints to avoid cold starts.
[08:56] Derrick: evictions — can you tune TTL per-session?
[09:00] Marcus: yes, TTLs are configurable and we expose metrics to set them based on session churn.
[09:06] [09:06] Eva: okay shifting to a quick scenario run: i'm going to compare two configs side-by-side — config A = small batch low prefetch, config B = medium batch 256-token prefetch + model fallback.
[09:20] [09:20] Marcus: results: config A median latency 210ms, p95 360ms, cost $X/1k; config B median 280ms p95 410ms cost $Y/1k (Y lower than X by ~22%).
[09:35] Sofia: config B p95 exceeds our 400ms target by a hair — is that acceptable?
[09:40] Marcus: you can tighten by 1) lowering batch max, 2) lowering prefetch window or 3) enabling fast-fallback to a smaller model for tail requests — that only slightly increases cost but keeps p95 in range.
[09:55] [09:55] Tom: what's the expected implementation effort for prefetch integration? our devs are stretched.
[10:01] Eva: prefetch is out-of-the-box for supported SDKs; most teams spend ~2-3 sprint days to wire session IDs and a small background worker. Marcus?
[10:10] Marcus: yep, dev work is mostly setting session affinity keys and optionally adding a background prefetch hook; we have sample code.
[10:20] [10:20] Derrick: any integration tests recommended?
[10:23] Dina: run load tests with synthetic reuse ratios and monitor wasted prefetch tokens vs hit-rate; console has a load-sim export to help.
[10:33] [10:33] Sofia: let's talk pricing transparency — if we do prefetch and get wasted tokens, how will that appear on invoices?
[10:40] Eva: itemized: compute tokens, prefetch tokens, and cache-savings credited as delta. we'll work with your finance team to audit early invoices.
[10:50] [10:50] (crosstalk) Priya: firewall detail again — will send the networking contacts.
[10:54] Marcus: perfect.
[11:00] [11:00] (longer pause while Marcus tweaks demo)
[11:36] Marcus: ok pulling up a different sim that models tool-heavy responses — notice batch size recommendation shrinks and prefetch window tightens.
[11:48] Derrick: makes sense. question: can we run the sim offline or as a CI job?
[11:52] Marcus: yes, there's a CLI version of the simulator and you can plug it into CI to ensure changes don't regress token economics.
[12:02] [12:02] Sofia: one more thing — retention and logging for GDPR. can we set log retention per workspace?
[12:08] Eva: yes, retention is configurable and we can mask PII; for private deployments it's under customer control.
[12:15] [12:15] Tom: ok, let's recap and agree next steps.
[12:19] Eva: recap: we'll send cost-sim spreadsheet and console links, Marcus will share runtime config and batching heuristics, Priya will provision sandbox access. we propose sandbox run week of 09/28 and a 90-min follow-up to review live hit-rates.
[12:35] Sofia: that works. thanks team.
[12:40] Tom: appreciated.
[12:43] Eva: excellent — i'll follow up with notes and the attachments.
[12:48] (meeting ends)
